1.q: Capacity 0? Re-put of an existing key? Get on a key that expired exactly now?
1.a: Reject 0 at construction; update in place + renew; now == expiry is expired

2.q: Complexity of Get, Put and the sweep?

Not the algorithm — the single lock

Lock — the invariant spans two structures

4.a: Shard by hash; hot key still one shard → front cache or approximate recency

prompts.label: Check my design — no code
prompts.text: I believe Dictionary<TKey, LinkedListNode<…>> plus a LinkedList for recency gives O(1) TryGet and Put, as long as the map and the list always hold exactly the same keys. Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?

prompts.label: Requirement change
prompts.text: The requirement changed: Add LruTtlCache<TKey,TValue>(capacity, IClock clock) with TryGet, Put(key, value, ttlMs) and Count. Expired at now >= expiry. A re-put renews the TTL. Prefer evicting an expired entry over a live one. List which members need to change and which do not, before writing any code.

flaw.ctx: You asked to make the LRU thread-safe.
flaw.answer: `ConcurrentDictionary` makes each *map* call atomic. The `LinkedList` is unprotected, and Get mutates it. Two Gets interleaving `Remove`/`AddFirst` corrupt the list; Put's check-then-evict is also a race. **Corrupted or threw in 20 of 20 stress trials.**
flaw.fix: One lock around each whole operation (SyncLruTtlCache). The invariant spans two structures, so the boundary does too.

qa.a: O(1) average for lookup, insert, remove; O(n) worst case if many keys collide. Enumeration is O(n) and order is not guaranteed.

Separate chaining, but without node objects: an `int[] buckets` of indices into an `Entry[]` array, each entry carrying its hash, key, value and a `next` index. Colliding keys form a chain through `next`.

When the entries array is full it grows to a larger prime (about double) and every entry is rehashed into new buckets — O(n) for that insert, amortised O(1). Pre-size with the constructor capacity when you know n.
Removing does not shrink anything: freed slots go on a free list for reuse. `TrimExcess()` shrinks. A struct key that is large is copied into every entry.
O(1) `Remove(node)`, `AddFirst`, `RemoveLast` given a `LinkedListNode<T>` handle. Storing the handle in the dictionary avoids an O(n) search.
No. Concurrent `Remove`/`AddFirst` corrupts its pointers (R3 corrupted in 20/20 runs).

Only code that locks the *same object*. `lock (x)` is `Monitor.Enter/Exit` on x's object header, in a try/finally. It also acts as a full memory barrier, so writes inside are visible to the next locker.
Yes, with two locks taken in different orders (D5), or with a call out to unknown code while holding the lock. One lock and no callouts cannot deadlock. `Monitor` is re-entrant for the same thread.

Uncontended, a lock is tens of nanoseconds. Contended, threads spin briefly then block, causing context switches; throughput collapses toward one thread's worth. The fix is less work under the lock, or more locks (striping).
`this`, a `Type`, a string — other code can lock them too. Use a private readonly object (or `System.Threading.Lock` in .NET 9+).
Each single call: `TryAdd`, `TryRemove`, `TryUpdate` (compare-and-swap on the value), `TryGetValue`, the indexer. `AddOrUpdate`/`GetOrAdd` atomically *store* — but see the next question.

qa.q: Does a read take a lock?
qa.a: No — reads are lock-free. Writes lock one stripe of buckets (lock striping), not the whole table. `Count` and `ToArray` take *all* the locks, so avoid them on a hot path.

qa.q: Is a read-modify-write across two calls safe?
qa.a: No. `TryGetValue` then `d[k] = v + 1` is check-then-act (debugging exercise D4 lost ~80% of increments). Use `AddOrUpdate`, or a `TryUpdate` loop.

qa.q: Do GetOrAdd / AddOrUpdate run the factory once?
qa.a: Not guaranteed: the delegate runs outside the lock and can run on several racing threads; only one result is stored. For an expensive factory, store `Lazy<T>` (review exercise R8).

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md: Build a key-value cache with a fixed capacity. When it is full and a new key arrives, evict the least recently used entry. Both reads and writes count as use. Then the requirements grow: entries expire, many threads call it, traffic reaches millions of requests.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- `TryGet(key, out value)` and `Put(key, value)`, both O(1)
- A read is a use — it changes the eviction order
- Re-putting an existing key updates it in place and counts as a use
- Capacity ≤ 0 is rejected at construction

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: Two jobs need two structures. A dictionary finds a key in O(1) but has no order. A linked list keeps order and moves a node in O(1) — if you already hold the node. Store the list node in the dictionary and you get both. Everything after that — TTL, threads, shards — is a change to one of those two structures, never a rewrite.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md: `Dictionary<TKey, LinkedListNode<…>>` for lookup; `LinkedList<…>` for recency, most recent at `First`. **Invariant: both hold exactly the same keys.** Every method that touches one touches the other before returning. That one sentence is also the synchronization boundary later.

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- Get: look up; if absent, miss. (TTL: if expired, remove from both and miss.) Move the node to the front. Return.
- Put: if present, update, move to front, return. If full, evict (TTL: prefer an expired entry near the cold end; else `Last`). Add to front and to the map.
- Sweep (TTL): walk at most *budget* nodes from the cold end, removing expired ones. Bounded work per call.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Type | Why |
|---|---|
| Dictionary<TKey, LinkedListNode<T>> | O(1) lookup that returns the list handle, so unlinking needs no search |
| LinkedList<T> | O(1) `Remove(node)`, `AddFirst`, `RemoveLast`; the BCL type is one less thing to get wrong than a hand-rolled list |
| IClock (injected) | Makes TTL testable without `Thread.Sleep` |
| object _gate + lock | The whole operation is the critical section, because a read writes |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
- Get: look up; if absent, miss. (TTL: if expired, remove from both and miss.) Move the node to the front. Return.
- Put: if present, update, move to front, return. If full, evict (TTL: prefer an expired entry near the cold end; else `Last`). Add to front and to the map.
- Sweep (TTL): walk at most *budget* nodes from the cold end, removing expired ones. Bounded work per call.

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md: Get and Put O(1). Sweep O(budget). Memory O(capacity) — but only if expired entries are reclaimed; that is why the sweep exists.

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
- Capacity two: put 1, put 2, get 1, put 3 → 2 is gone, 1 survives (a read is a use).
- Re-put updates in place: count unchanged, new value returned.
- Capacity one: the newest key always wins.
- TTL: live at 99 ms, dead at exactly 100 ms — test the boundary, not one past it.
- An expired entry is reclaimed on read (count drops).
- Eviction prefers an expired entry over a live LRU one.
- Sweep honours its budget: 1,000 expired entries, budget 100 → exactly 100 reclaimed.
- 8 threads × 20,000 mixed operations: count never exceeds capacity, no torn values.
- Resize 4 → 2 keeps the two hottest; resize up admits more.

learn.md:

- 1 kept
- update does not grow count
- updated value
- capacity 1 keeps the newest
- capacity 0 rejected
- miss returns false

**S3 — Concurrent access**

- no exception under 8 threads (

- keeps the two hottest
- growing admits more

learn.title: 11 · AI usage strategy
learn.md:
- Write the interface and the two field declarations yourself; ask only for the method bodies.
- For TTL: "Add per-entry TTL using the injected IClock. Do not change eviction. List the members that change first."
- For threads: use the concurrency template — ask for the breaking interleaving, then decide the boundary yourself.

**Prompts for this question:**

- *Check my design — no code* — "I believe Dictionary<TKey, LinkedListNode<…>> plus a LinkedList for recency gives O(1) TryGet and Put, as long as the map and the list always hold exactly the same keys. Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?"
- *Review, do not rewrite* — "Review my implementation for correctness and edge cases. Do not rewrite the code. List problems most severe first, each with the input that triggers it."
- *Race conditions* — "Now review this implementation for race conditions if multiple threads call TryGet and Put concurrently. For each race, give the interleaving that breaks it. Then name the smallest synchronization boundary that preserves correctness. Do not write code yet."
- *Tests that expose bugs* — "Suggest tests that could expose bugs in my implementation: boundaries, duplicates, empty and invalid input, and concurrency where it applies. For each, say why the expected value is correct."
- *Complexity check* — "What is the time and space complexity of each public method as written? Do not claim a bound unless every step achieves it."
- *Requirement change* — "The requirement changed: Add LruTtlCache<TKey,TValue>(capacity, IClock clock) with TryGet, Put(key, value, ttlMs) and Count. Expired at now >= expiry. A re-put renews the TTL. Prefer evicting an expired entry over a live one. List which members need to change and which do not, before writing any code."

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- Swapping in `ConcurrentDictionary` and calling it thread-safe (R3).
- Get not moving the node to the front (R1) — passes put/get tests, fails eviction-after-read.
- TTL with expired entries left in place: returns -1 correctly, leaks memory, and evicts live entries first (R2).
- `DateTime.Now` instead of an injected clock — tests then need `Thread.Sleep`.
- A full-map sweep under the lock (R10).

**Verification exercise:** Race condition — `ConcurrentDictionary` makes each *map* call atomic. The `LinkedList` is unprotected, and Get mutates it. Two Gets interleaving `Remove`/`AddFirst` corrupt the list; Put's check-then-evict is also a race. **Corrupted or threw in 20 of 20 stress trials.**

learn.title: 13 · Concurrency considerations
learn.md:
Shared state: the map and the list. The invariant spans both, so they must change together — one critical section per operation. Two threads in Get on different keys both call `_order.Remove` and `AddFirst`; without a lock the list's internal pointers interleave and corrupt. That is exactly what review exercise R3 does in 20/20 trials.

**Level 3 — Concurrency**

- *Two threads call Get on different keys at once. What shared state do they touch?* — Both move nodes in one list: map + list invariant → one critical section
- *Lock or ConcurrentDictionary?* — Lock — the invariant spans two structures
- *Can this deadlock? Can the lock become a bottleneck?* — One lock, no callouts → no deadlock; yes under contention → shard

learn.title: 14 · Scalability considerations
learn.md:
**Level 4 — Scale**

- *100× traffic, one hot key.* — Shard by hash; hot key still one shard → front cache or approximate recency
- *Memory pressure.* — Byte-weighted capacity; Resize down

learn.title: 15 · Production considerations
learn.md:
- Bound memory: capacity in entries is not bytes — for variable-size values, cap by weight.
- Hit ratio, eviction rate, expired-on-read rate as metrics; alert on hit-ratio drop.
- A slow source behind the cache: collapse concurrent misses (cache the in-flight `Lazy`), and add a timeout.
- Warm-up after deploy: a cold cache is a thundering herd on the source.

**Level 5 — Productionisation**

- *What do you measure and alert on?* — Hit ratio (relative drop), evictions by reason, lock wait, size
- *The source behind it goes down.* — Serve stale with a bound, circuit breaker, collapse concurrent misses
- *What happens during a deploy?* — Cold cache → stampede on the source; warm up or ramp traffic

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
- *Implement LRU.* — Dictionary of list nodes + linked list. State the invariant. Test eviction after a read.
- *Resize it at runtime.* — Shrinking evicts immediately — expired first, then from the cold end — until Count ≤ the new capacity. Growing just raises the bound. `Resize` in the listing; tested both ways.
- *Add TTL.* — Absolute expiry per entry, injected clock, lazy check on read. Re-put renews. Decide and say whether an expired entry counts toward capacity until reclaimed.
- *Make it thread-safe.* — One lock around each operation, because Get mutates the list. Reject `ConcurrentDictionary` alone — it protects the map, not the list.
- *Millions of requests.* — The lock serialises everything. Shard by key hash, N independent caches. Each shard is exact LRU; the whole is approximate. Measure the hit-ratio cost.
- *Expired-entry memory growth.* — Lazy expiry alone leaks keys that are never read again. Add a bounded sweep from the cold end, on a timer or piggy-backed on writes. Never a full scan under the lock.
- *Memory limits, not entry counts.* — Entries vary in size: track a byte weight per entry and evict until under a byte budget. Under memory pressure (GC notifications, a container limit), Resize down.
- *Hot keys and high contention.* — One hot key lands on one shard and one lock. Options: a small per-thread or read-replicated front cache for the hottest keys, or approximate recency so reads stop writing.
- *Observability.* — Hit ratio, eviction rate split by reason (capacity vs expiry), expired-on-read rate, lock wait time, size in entries and bytes. Alert on a relative hit-ratio drop.
- *Distribute it.* — Consistent hashing across nodes; a client-side or proxy router; replication only if a miss is expensive. This is now a design question — Memcached/Redis Cluster, and say when you would just use one.

**Level 1 — Correctness**

- *Capacity 0? Re-put of an existing key? Get on a key that expired exactly now?* — Reject 0 at construction; update in place + renew; now == expiry is expired

**Level 2 — Complexity**

- *Complexity of Get, Put and the sweep?* — O(1), O(1), O(budget) — and why the sweep is bounded
- *Where is the bottleneck?* — Not the algorithm — the single lock

aiGuide.intro: Five requirements arrive one at a time: LRU, then a TTL per entry, then threads, then memory, then resize. The design and the lock boundary are yours; the list surgery is what you hand over.
plan: Restate, ask: is a read a use? what does a miss return? capacity 0?
Write the fields and signatures; three tests (evict-after-read, update, capacity 1)
AI fills in TryGet/Put against your class → review → run
TTL: you add ExpiresAt + IClock and decide the boundary; AI edits; boundary test
Threads: you name the lock boundary; AI applies it and writes the stress test
Memory and resize: bounded sweep, shrink; AI reviews complexity
Scale: sharding and its trade-off — talk, no code

stages.name: LRU cache
stages.yours: Say the design out loud, then write it as fields: `Dictionary<TKey, LinkedListNode<Entry>>` for lookup and `LinkedList<Entry>` for recency, most recent first. The invariant: **the map and the list hold the same keys**. The rule people forget: **a TryGet is a use**. Signatures throw NotImplementedException.
stages.ai: **Co-generate.** The design is fixed in your fields; the remaining work is list surgery that you can check in a minute. That is exactly what to delegate.
bad: Implement an LRU cache in C#.
The LeetCode answer: `LRUCache` with int keys, `Get` returning -1 for a miss, its own field names.
No class pasted, so it invents its own API — your tests stop compiling
It never says whether a read counts as a use, so you cannot tell if it knew
good:
C#. Implement TryGet and Put in the LruCache<TKey,TValue> below. O(1) each, using my Dictionary and LinkedList node handles. A TryGet counts as a use: move the node to the front. When full, evict the least recently used. Keep my fields; no new public members; no thread-safety yet. List your assumptions first. Show only the two methods.
<LruCache.cs pasted>
**Rule** spelled out: a read is a use
**Shape** frozen, so your tests still compile
**"No thread-safety yet"** keeps the reply small
**Assumptions first** — a wrong reading shows up as one sentence
stages.reply: Typical defect: **TryGet returns the value but never moves the node**, while Put does. It passes put-then-get, and fails the first eviction-after-read test.
validate: Capacity 1: the second Put evicts the first
Put of an existing key updates the value, keeps Count, and makes it most recent
A miss returns false and does not touch the list
No loop over the list anywhere — every path is O(1)
stages.fix: Two lines (move the node inside TryGet) → **fix it by hand**. Faster than a prompt, and it shows you understood.
stages.say: "TryGet didn't refresh recency, so the key I just read was evicted. My eviction-after-read test caught it; I moved the node myself."
stages.say_iv: Implement an LRU cache. Get and Put should both be O(1).

stages.name: Every entry has a TTL
stages.yours: Add `ExpiresAt` to the entry and take an `IClock` in the constructor. Decide three rules before prompting: expiry is checked **lazily on read** (O(1)); an entry is **dead at the expiry instant** (`now >= ExpiresAt`); a re-put **renews** the TTL.
stages.ai: **Co-generate** the edits to TryGet and Put. The rules are decided; the changes are small and local.
bad: One TTL for the whole cache, `DateTime.UtcNow`, and a `Timer` that sweeps the dictionary every second.
The question says **per entry**; it built one global TTL
The timer runs on another thread and changes the dictionary with **no lock**
Removing while iterating the dictionary throws
`DateTime.UtcNow` ignores your clock, so no test can control time
good: Add a TTL per entry: Put(key, value, ttlMs). Use my injected IClock — no DateTime, no timers. An entry is dead when now >= ExpiresAt: TryGet then returns false and removes it. A re-put renews the TTL. When full, prefer evicting an expired entry near the cold end. Change only what the TTL needs. Keep my other methods unchanged. State your assumptions first.
**Exclusions** by name: no DateTime, no timers — the two wrong designs
Says what happens to the dead entry: **removed on read**
**Size**: "change only what the TTL needs" protects your stage-1 code
stages.reply: Typical defect: **`now > ExpiresAt`** — alive at exactly the TTL. Or it returns false for an expired key but **leaves it in the map**, where it still counts against capacity.
validate: At ttl−1 alive; at exactly ttl dead
Reading an expired key removes it — Count drops
A re-put before expiry renews it
Full cache with one expired entry: the expired one is evicted, not a live one
stages.fix: `>` → `>=` is one character → **by hand**. A missing removal is two lines → by hand.
stages.say: "Expiry is lazy, so it costs nothing until a read. Dead at the expiry instant — my boundary test pins it."
stages.require: Add `LruTtlCache<TKey,TValue>(capacity, IClock clock)` with `TryGet`, `Put(key, value, ttlMs)` and `Count`. Expired at `now >= expiry`. A re-put renews the TTL. Prefer evicting an expired entry over a live one.
stages.say_iv: Now every entry has a time-to-live. An expired entry must read as a miss.

stages.name: Concurrent access
stages.yours: Decide the boundary yourself and say it: **TryGet writes** (it moves a node), so one lock must cover the map **and** the list, for the whole operation. Concurrent collections cannot help: the invariant spans two structures.
stages.ai: **Co-generate** the locking, and let the AI write the **stress test** — the best delegation in the round: boilerplate you can check by reading its invariant.
bad: `ConcurrentDictionary`, list unprotected. A real stress run throws "The LinkedList node does not belong to current LinkedList".
The map is safe; **the list is not**, and TryGet writes to it
Put's check-then-evict is still a race
It reads as an upgrade, which is why it is the most common wrong answer
good: Make the cache thread-safe with one private lock around the whole of TryGet, Put, SweepExpired and Count — TryGet also writes, it moves a node. Keep the plain Dictionary; no ConcurrentDictionary. Then write a stress test: 8 threads, 20,000 mixed Put/TryGet each over keys 0–199; assert no exception, Count ≤ capacity, and every value read equals its key. Keep my fields and signatures. Explain in one line why each method needs the lock. Show only the changed methods and the test.
Asks for a test with an **invariant**, not "it didn't crash"
stages.reply: With this prompt the code is usually right. **Check the test instead**: do the threads really overlap (Parallel.For or a Barrier), and does it assert something a race would break?
validate: Every public method takes the same lock — Count included
Nothing slow or external runs inside the lock
The stress test asserts an invariant: Count ≤ capacity, no torn values
Say the cost: every thread queues on one lock — next step is sharding
stages.fix: If it gave you ConcurrentDictionary: **reject it with the reason**, then send the good prompt. Do not patch it.
stages.say: "The invariant spans the map and the list, so the lock has to cover both. If one lock becomes the bottleneck, I'd shard by key — each shard exact LRU, the whole cache approximately."
stages.require: Add `SyncLruTtlCache<TKey,TValue>(capacity, IClock)` — the same API, safe under concurrent callers.
stages.say_iv: Multiple threads now call TryGet and Put at the same time. Where is the shared state, and where exactly is your synchronization boundary?
